Sports.title: World Cup final: Trump, half-time show and everything but the football – live
Sports.content:
10m ago 17.25 EDT As things stand, Cape Verde have scored more goals against Argentina than Spain and England combined. Share

13m ago 17.23 EDT The hafltime show lasted just over 27 minutes. So we’ll have seen Animal drumming for almost as long as we’ll watch extra time. I know that’s incredibly strained but I’m killing time until Trump grabs the trophy at the presentation ceremony and runs away laughing. Share

33m ago 17.02 EDT Trump is shown looking quite animated in the executive box. By this point in the NBA finals, he had nodded off to sleep. Share

38m ago 16.58 EDT The news is in: the World Cup final is a sell-out. The New York Jets have sold out this stadium, so I’m not sure that counts as an achievement. Share

41m ago 16.54 EDT Phil Udell writes in: “I’m a big fan of Coldplay’s efforts to be an ethically sound modern stadium band but how does that sit with allying themselves with such a questionable organisation as Fifa, to say nothing of their pal in the White House?” I imagine they’ll point out that the halftime show was to promote Fifa’s charity efforts. But … good point. Nathan North: “If the score is still 0-0 at the end of extra time, instead of the lottery of penalties, I think the only fair thing to do would be to give the World Cup to the winner of the third place match.” Share

45m ago 16.51 EDT Trump wasn’t shown on the video screen at the stadium during the halftime show – Fifa is smart enough not to offer a distraction. We did see Carlos Alcaraz, Serena Williams and Zidane though – none of whom were booed. How could you boo Carlos anyway? Share

54m ago 16.41 EDT Facundo Iglesia is in Buenos Aires for us. Here’s how things are going there: A small screen hanging outside a travel agency in downtown Buenos Aires draws a crowd of hundreds. If the sound is even on, it’s drowned out by the monotone drone of vuvuzelas, the crackle of firecrackers, and the fans chanting: “El que no salta es español” (“Anyone who doesn’t jump is a Spaniard”) and the better-known but less appropriate version, “El que no salta es un inglés” (“Anyone who doesn’t jump is an Englishman”). Thousands across the capital are watching the final this way - people in Albiceleste jerseys wandering the area around the Obelisco, catching glimpses of TVs inside or outside businesses, jumping and shouting as if they were at East Rutherford Stadium in New Jersey. But those scattered pockets of fans carry a well-known risk: spoilers. Broadcast delays across TV channels and radio stations are a running annoyance in Argentina, and a group of supporters reacting to a play will sometimes tip off another group nearby - before the play has even happened for them. A respectful round of applause, for instance - later revealed to be for Lisandro “Licha” Martínez leaving the pitch - rippled down the block a full beat before the screen outside an empanada shop caught up. “It’s annoying - that’s why I’m watching the screen with commentary on my phone,” says Carla Lucía del Pardo, a 31-year-old pastry chef. “That way, I gain five seconds.” For Del Pardo, Argentina is playing “well, but too calm.” “They’re defending the goal, but not really going on the attack,” she added. Share Updated at 16.42 EDT

1h ago 16.32 EDT Reader verdicts on the half-time show Gillian Forrester: “You did not mention that the fabulous Gustavo Dudamel was conducting! He’s moving to the NY Phil this fall (and is Venezuelan, FYI).” Matthew Leung: “I hope that is the only World Cup half-time show I ever have to see in my life. 17 minutes of underwhelming, cringeworthy crap. I am a BTS fan, but this wasn’t really a great ad for them.” Brigid Brennan: “Did I hear some boos for Pele when he appeared on screen? (From Argentinian fans, presumably). It was a choice to have a heavy Brazilian influence in front of a pro Argentinian crowd - Ronaldo, Ronaldinho & Pele.” Philip Reed: “For three decades soccer fandom in the US, both MLS and especially international club, has had a strong undercurrent of, ‘This is the sport that it’s OK to care about and still be somewhat artsy’. It’s also why there’s little overlap of say watching Premier League games at 8am with the “soccer mom” culture of piling the kids in the SUV and remembering to bring the orange slices for halftime. They’re just two different sets of cultural signifiers. Maybe this World Cup will merge the two a bit.” Leo Addor: “The thing was going well until they brought on Ted Lasso and then Bieber. Bieber seemed like a homeless guy who cut up his own clothes and then wandered onto the pitch to play guitar about some weird Christian bullshit (which is basically accurate). “Burna Boy seemed like he was contractually obligated to stay at least 1/2 feet away from Shakira at all times. Their dynamic was weird. “They showed Dua Lipa watching afterwards. She seemed to think that she could’ve done better, and well, she’s right.” Share Updated at 16.34 EDT

1h ago 16.22 EDT I’m not sure how much the players would have enjoyed trying to keep themselves warmed up during that extended break. Maybe Messi, 56, had a nice nap. Maybe there was a unifying theme to that halftime show – probably something to do with football uniting the world – but Bad Bunny it was not. Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl half-time show review – a thrilling ode to Boricua joy Read more Share

1h ago 16.20 EDT Wayne Rooney gives his verdict on the half-time show ... “I like a lot of them artists but I thought it was crap.” Don’t ever change, Wayne. Roy Keane liked Shakira. Share Updated at 16.38 EDT

1h ago 16.17 EDT And so, we go back to the football. Were the professional singers who performed professional? Yes! Were the cute kids who performed cute? Yes! Did anyone ask for this? No! Did this add to the World Cup final? Not really! Will it convert neutral American fans to soccer? No! Would an exciting game without a big interruption in the middle do a better job of that? Yes! What I’m saying is that they should just have shown highlights of England 6-4 France from yesterday instead. Animal was good though. View image in fullscreen The best bit of the halftime show. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters Share Updated at 16.18 EDT

1h ago 16.14 EDT A kids choir from Staten Island – who says nothing good comes out of Staten Island – are joined by Kermit and Miss Piggy next. Shakira has such affection for Staten Island that she comes along to join them. And Chris Martin, who is curating this show. This is very wholesome and nice and professionally done. Does the World Cup final need it … probably not? Share

1h ago 16.11 EDT Shakira and Burna Boy are next up. They bring on some cute kids to dance, which – understandably – goes down well with the crowd. Share

1h ago 16.10 EDT Bieber shows his improv skills by adding “World Cup” to the lyrics of his song. They don’t pay him the big bucks for nothing (he’s playing for free, for charity) Share

1h ago 16.09 EDT Alexander Abnos I am running the TV broadcast of this halftime show alongside watching it live at the stadium and, unsurprisingly, this stuff absolutely does not translate live. It took til halfway through Seven Nation Army for me to realize Animal was playing the drums. View image in fullscreen The Muppets at the World Cup final. Obviously. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters Share Updated at 16.11 EDT

1h ago 16.08 EDT Here comes Ted Lasso and Coach Beard to introduce …Justin Bieber. Bieber is 32 now, so is unlikely to win a professional football contract. Good voice though! Share

1h ago 16.06 EDT BTS are their usual professional, excellent selves as they belt out Dynamite. They may have played one or two stadium gigs in their time. They get more air time than Madonna, but fewer Brazilian World Cup winners. Share Updated at 16.07 EDT

2h ago 16.05 EDT Animal is on the drums as they play Seven Nation Army. OK, this is now an excellent halftime show. Forget any previous criticism I had of it. In fact, just stop it here. After a quick Viking Row, BTS are on – with no Animal. Share

2h ago 16.04 EDT And we’re on Madonna is on a car driven by Ronaldo (the Brazilian one) and … Ronaldinho. I hope they have travel insurance because that car doesn’t look that roadworthy. They’re driving on to the field now. Ronaldo looks very happy to be there. Share

2h ago 16.02 EDT They’ve rolled out a big tarp at the New York New Jersey Stadium as they prepare the field for the performance. It’s been a great day for tarps at today’s final. Share

2h ago 15.58 EDT Just a reminder that the halftime show will last 25 to 30 minutes. Around 11 minutes for the actual show and the rest of the time to set up the stage and then take it all down. There are worries that the added down time for players could lead to injuries as muscles cool down due to inactivity. On the upside, they’ll get to hear Justin Bieber sing for about 90 seconds. The list of artists includes: Shakira; Burna Boy; BTS; Madonna; Kermit and Miss Piggy; conductor Gustavo Dudamel with musicians from the New York Philharmonic and the Simon Bolivar Symphony Orchestra of Venezuela; dance troupe Ghetto Kids; Emmanuel Kelly; PS 22 Chorus (cute kids from a local school). Share

2h ago 15.56 EDT Alexander Abnos The half-time show approaches, which means uber-warmup man Michael “Let’s Get Ready To Rumble” Buffer is back, and he is yelling very loud. Talk about someone who should be booed Share Updated at 16.39 EDT

2h ago 15.47 EDT Does the World Cup final need a halftime show? The argument for the halftime show seems to be that it’s what new fans want. James Massing of Live Nation, who are helping put on the show, told the BBC that sports events need to change things up because they are “competing with any other live experience - going to the museum, going to the theatre, going to the cinema”. I’m pretty sure no one going to the museum expects a halftime show though, and people are still happy to queue up to see the Mona Lisa without one. I suspect that this is also a push by people who think that US fans will refuse to watch a big event unless it has a halftime show, even though plenty of big sporting events, from the NBA finals to the World Series don’t have halftime shows. I actually think the appeal of soccer to many Americans is that it’s not the NFL, in the same way that many European fans enjoy the NFL because it’s not soccer. And people expect a halftime show at the Super Bowl because it’s the Super Bowl, not because they expect - or want - one at a World Cup final. Added to that, the best Super Bowl halftime shows often provide commentary on the state of America, from Bad Bunny’s hymn to immigrants at this year’s Super Bowl to Beyonce’s black panther tribute in 2016. Somehow, I doubt Gianni and friends are going to allow Shakira to sneak in references to the Iran War today. On the upside, all the artists are performing for free, there will be a kids choir and the show is meant to support Fifa’s education fund. Share

2h ago 15.30 EDT Sam Jones Madrid’s Plaza de Colón, famous for its massive Spanish flag, is absolutely rammed as the match begins. Police are turning people away from the barriers that have been installed around the square, but the mood inside it somewhere between expectant and buoyant. No one wants to hex the game but hopes are high.



“It’s a historic moment and it’s really exciting,” said Katy, 18, who was two years old the last time Spain won the World Cup. “I’m obviously hoping that Spain win and I think it’ll be 3-2 to Spain.” Miguel Hinojal Vicente, 37, had come to Madrid from Toledo as much for the party atmosphere as for the match itself. Unlike Katy, he had vivid memories of Spain’s last World Cup triumph. “Shit, it was just a magical thing,” he said. “But, to tell the truth, I’m more of a Atleti fan than a Spain fan.” His friend Raquel Garcia was a little more enthusiastic - and optimistic. She predicted a 3-0 win for Spain, with two goals in the first half and one in the second. But it was about more than just football for her. “This is about the hopes of a country and it’s about unity,” she said. “Events like these bring people together and they make people happy.” Share

2h ago 15.25 EDT Rusty Shpork gets in touch: “Are any of the online prediction markets taking bets on the exact minute Trump nods off? I’m going with the 27th minute, after he’s exhausted himself rage-bleating on Truth Social during the first commercial break about the large number of “probably illegal” Latinos in the stadium. If Spain win, Trump will probably try to present the trophy to Messi, anyway. Brand recognition, yada yada.” Share

2h ago 15.22 EDT The TV cameras show Will Ferrell in the stands before cutting to Pharell Williams. I don’t know if that was deliberate but the Fereell/Pharell cut was sonically pleasing. Share

3h ago 15.02 EDT The Spanish national anthem is being played by a Spanish brass band. A lovely, slow number that perhaps doesn’t lead to the high intensity rendition you want in a huge moment. I bet the Argentina one will be a bit more peppy … it is! Argentinian singer Maria Becerra leads the fans in the stands to a rousing rendition. All the Spanish fans got was some dudes with some tubas and trumpets. Way more Argentinian fans than Spaniards in the crowd, by the way. Kick off is already two minutes late, by the way… Share

3h ago 14.55 EDT Alexander Abnos The Spanish and Argentinian fans absolutely do not care about any of this. About halfway through, they have started singing their own songs and drowning out whatever it is that Tom Cruise is going on about. Share

3h ago 14.54 EDT Tom Cruise is out to do some acting! He is playing a man in a tight black t-shirt telling us a story about the World Cup being good. This is great acting because he is convincing as a man in a tight black t-shirt telling us a story about the World Cup being good. He even shows his versatility by saying the teams are España and Argentina. He does not jump off a high place or do anything with wires or creep us out by jumping on a sofa though. Can’t have everything. Share Updated at 14.56 EDT

3h ago 14.52 EDT Here’s Carlos Alcaraz! With the World Cup trophy and World Cup winners Andres Iniesta and Marrio Kempes. The stadium announcer makes sure to tell us that it’s presented by some luxury brand or other. Share

3h ago 14.48 EDT Trump is shown on the TV and appears to be booed, although that could just have been people booing Robbie Williams, who is now singing along with Nicole Scherzinger and Laura Pausini. Trump wasn’t shown on the jumbotron at the stadium, so I’m assuming maybe people just don’t like Robbie – and the poor guy hasn’t even started any wars (yet?). Share Updated at 14.50 EDT

3h ago 14.47 EDT And here’s the Star-Spangled Banner. World class singer Jennifer Hudson somewhat unsurprisingly sings it very well. Is the band out of sync? Maybe, but these anthem performances are often so extravagant, I’m never sure if they’re supposed to be like that. Anyway, headline: Jennifer Hudson can sing. Share

3h ago 14.43 EDT And now the second-half of the closing ceremony (yes, there are two halfs of this) starts. Jennifer Hudson will sing the Star-Spangled Banner. Actually, it’s been delayed – I suspect this match may not be kicking off on time… Share

3h ago 14.40 EDT ITV reports that there has been a glitch with the ticketing system, meaning there have been delays for some of the fans who have paid eye-watering sums to get to this match today. There are still a few empty seats in the stands… Share

3h ago 14.38 EDT Donald Trump has managed to sneak into the stadium without any fans noticing: View image in fullscreen The Marine One helicopter carrying Donald Trump, and an escort helicopter, fly over the stadium. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Share

3h ago 14.35 EDT Bob O’Hara writes in: “Just catching up, and that building Alexander Abnos couldn’t recognise? Could it be Trump Tower?” That would make sense given Gianni’s preferences … Share

3h ago 14.34 EDT Professional Spain fan and sometime actor Javier Bardem is here today. View image in fullscreen Javier Bardem arrives for the match. Photograph: Arturo Holmes/FIFA/Getty Images Share

3h ago 14.28 EDT If you think the various controversies that have engulfed Fifa president Gianni Infantino during this World Cup – from his Peace Prize for Donald Trump to the suspension of Folarin Balogun’s red card to the high price of tickets – will have any negative effect on his reign, then think again. The fact is that he is very good at making money for Fifa, and that’s enough for most of the organization’s representatives. Here’s a little more on the subject in our video explainer: Scandal-proof: why Infantino's Fifa power can't be touched – video Share

3h ago 14.22 EDT An organization called The Final Red Card is arranging a protest around today’s final. According to the organization: “During today’s Fifa World Cup Final, thousands of fans are expected to raise commemorative referee-style red cards in a coordinated, peaceful visual action during the tournament’s trophy presentation, transforming soccer’s most universally recognized symbol into a global call for democracy, accountability, and a repudiation of Trump’s corruption. “The action, titled The Final Red Card, is being organized by a coalition of artists, organizers, and advocacy organizations led by SoundsGood, the campaign activation studio behind the nationally covered Flags in the Stands: ICE OUT activation during Super Bowl LX, together with Contra-ICE, Make the Road New Jersey, 50501, People vs. The Machine, South Asians for America, Way to Win, Movement Voter Project, and additional national and local partners.” Share

3h ago 14.18 EDT Alexander Abnos Marine One has just flown over the stadium with two escort helicopters Share

3h ago 14.14 EDT Weather watch The New York area has been swamped by smoke from Canadian wildfires for much of the last few days but, after storms last night, the air is clear (by local standards). Temperatures will be around 82F/28C at kickoff, nowhere near as sweltering as we saw for France v Paraguay or England v Norway, so it’s unlikely conditions will affect the players – particularly as Spanish and Argentinians players will be used to playing in the heat. Share

3h ago 14.06 EDT Alexander Abnos The White House press pool has arrived at the stadium, which caused the temporary closure of every ramp and staircase on the north side of the stadium. The president is presumably quite close by. Share

4h ago 13.59 EDT Streamer IShowSpeed, probably more famous than 98% of the players at this World Cup, is performing too. It’s probably not even watching the match now that he’s been on. View image in fullscreen IShowSpeed performs during the closing ceremony. Photograph: Héctor Vivas/FIFA/Getty Images Share

4h ago 13.56 EDT Post Malone has rocked up to perform at the closing ceremony, which is now taking place. Swae Lee joins him for toe tapper Sunflower. View image in fullscreen Post Malone and Swae Lee perform during the closing ceremony. Photograph: Alex Pantling/FIFA/Getty Images Share

4h ago 13.53 EDT Just a reminder that the halftime show will last 25 to 30 minutes. Around 11 minutes for the actual show and the rest of the time to set up the stage and then take it all down. There are worries that the added down time for players could lead to injuries as muscles cool down due to inactivity. On the upside, they’ll get to hear Justin Bieber sing for about 90 seconds. The list of artists includes: Shakira; Burna Boy; BTS; Madonna; Kermit and Miss Piggy; conductor Gustavo Dudamel with musicians from the New York Philharmonic and the Simon Bolivar Symphony Orchestra of Venezuela; dance troupe Ghetto Kids; Emmanuel Kelly; PS 22 Chorus (cute kids from a local school). Share Updated at 14.33 EDT

4h ago 13.46 EDT Facundo Iglesia is on the ground for us in Buenos Aires to take in the atmosphere among Argentina fans: Argentines can’t be accused of tempering their trademark intensity – or their superstitions – in the hours leading up to the World Cup final. On the eve of the match, thousands of people - mostly parents with their children – flocked to Buenos Aires’ Parque Rivadavia to trade or buy Panini stickers, racing to fill their albums just in time. Many tucked stickers of the Spanish players into freezers, an accessible, popularized bit of witchcraft meant to curse the opposing squad. Now, on the day of the final, under a persistent drizzle, hundreds are waving flags and blowing vuvuzelas at the Obelisco - the city’s designated meeting point to celebrate the national team, whatever the result may be. The streets leading to the monument are packed with fans and street vendors hawking flags, face paint, and plastic ponchos. María de las Nieves López, a Paraguayan pizzeria owner who traveled from Ezeiza, a city 35 kilometers outside the capital, wasn’t fazed by the rain or the lack of a screen near the monument. “It’s Lio [Messi]’s last one. We wanted to come and cheer him and the rest of the squad on - to support them from here. We’ll watch the game on our phones if we have to,” she said. López, who has lived in the country for 25 years, carried a 20-year-old doll she credits with bringing “good luck,” because it “had watched all the games.” “Well, we’ve been winning so far,” she said. “I promised her that, if Argentina wins the final, I’ll buy her a new dress.” Share

4h ago 13.41 EDT The closing ceremony is off to a good start. Or rather not start at all. It was supposed to get underway 90 mins before kickoff but is yet to do so. There are often delays when Donald Trump attends sporting events as the arena is secured. It’s unclear as yet whether kickoff will be delayed. I’m sure they can scrap some bits of this closing ceremony to hurry things along. No one will mind if Robbie Williams is bumped, surely? Share

4h ago 13.38 EDT Alexander Abnos is at the stadium for us, and has some team news (sort of): Spain have just entered the stadium and are wandering around in the center of the field. A team of Fifa volunteers are gathered holding what looks to be a very large tarp, which presumably will be a key part of the closing ceremony. I think Spain team may have to move.... View image in fullscreen The world’s most famous tarp in action. Photograph: Elsa/Getty Images And here comes the tarp! It’s an artistic and frankly kinda tacky composite of a number of New York City landmarks. Clockwise from bottom left on your TV screens: The new Calatrava train hub at World Trade Center, 1 World Trade, The Brooklyn Bridge, the Empire State Building, The Vessel, some building I don’t recognize, the Guggenheim, the Chrysler Building, the Statue of Liberty, 30 Rock, the Washington Square arch, the Flatiron building. Share Updated at 13.43 EDT

4h ago 13.36 EDT Good news from Fifa! There will be a “fan-centric pre-match ceremony” today, which means “an immersive, 360-degree concept that transforms the stadium into a shared stage. No matter where supporters are seated, each will have a distinct and engaging perspective, with extra-large country flag banners and on-pitch elements carefully positioned to involve the crowd in an authentic and meaningful way.” I bet there’s a hologram. There is always a hologram. It gets better though. At long last, Fifa is going to pay attention to its poor, neglected sponsors: “the youth programme and players’ tunnel will feature both traditional and new integrations of FIFA’s Commercial Partners, thanks to the involvement of adidas, Coca-Cola, Kia, Mengniu, Qatar Airways and Quaker.” At first, I read that as “quakers” and I was expecting a silent prayer meeting, which would have been quite nice. The pre-match ceremony will also include “additional elements such as coloured smoke or pyrotechnics.” Coloured smoke OR pyrotechnics? $5,000 a ticket and you don’t even get both? This better be a good game. Share

Sports.title: Kane says Tuchel will ‘learn a lot’ from England pressures after exit to Argentina
Sports.content:
Harry Kane has backed Thomas Tuchel to learn from England’s World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina and believes they must use the forthcoming Nations League campaign to gain experience of playing against the top teams.

Kane was an unused substitute as England sealed third place with an entertaining 6-4 victory against France on Saturday – their best finish at a World Cup on foreign soil. Tuchel, who signed a contract extension before the tournament, has been criticised heavily for his tactics against Argentina when he opted to switch to a back five to try to defend a 1-0 lead.

Kane admitted England had fallen short against Lionel Scaloni’s side but described the environment Tuchel has created since succeeding Gareth Southgate in 2025 as “the best England group I’ve been a part of in terms of togetherness”.

The captain said: “I know there are a lot of questions after the other night. We have to process it as players. I’m sure the manager will. It’s his first major tournament. He’ll learn a lot from the players, the situations, the pressures, the travel.

“There are also a lot of things as players we can learn from the other night. For now it’s just trying to process everything. We had a lot of good things, a lot of tough situations we overcame. The group is incredible, the best England group I’ve been a part of in terms of togetherness. The boss was a big part of creating that as well.

“Fans are going to be angry and we understand it. It’s a major tournament and that’s why you dream so big. When it doesn’t go your way you have to take the criticism. We’re all willing to do that, to dare to reach the biggest goal of all. We know over the next two years until we’re facing that situation again there is always going to be a question mark. It’s something we have to take and use as motivation.”

England missed out on facing regular top-class opposition in the buildup to the World Cup after being relegated from the top Nations League group in 2022 under Southgate. They were promoted in 2024 and will face Spain, Croatia and Czechia, starting with a rematch of the Euro 2024 final against Luis de la Fuente’s side on 26 September at Wembley. After beating France – albeit in a largely meaningless game – Kane thinks England must take the competition seriously if they are to thrive in tournaments.

View image in fullscreen Defeat to an established opponent was a familiar feeling for England. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

“The last 30 minutes of Argentina is not the team we want to be,” he said. “We spent a lot of time over the last two years talking about that situation, to attack those moments. The bottom line is we lost anyway. It’s easy to go away and talk about it. We need to get better at actually being in those situations. We can train, play the qualifiers … I think the Nations League will be big for us, against Spain and Croatia, big teams.

“Getting used to those big environments and finding our best form against those teams, like we did against France, albeit not in the most competitive match. We have to learn, improve. The coach will have improved from these learnings. I can talk as much as I want but ultimately it’s about showing it next time we’re in that situation.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Kane has been on the losing side in two World Cup semi-finals and two European Championship finals and he believes Tuchel is the man to help England to make the final step.

“The enthusiasm he has, the emotion he brings, the tactical experience he has … it doesn’t mean you’re going to get it right every time. We want to get it right on the biggest occasions and he expects that from himself as well. He’s a fantastic coach. He not only gave the players belief but he gave the country belief that it was our year. That is why it hurts even more than other years because everyone believed we were going all the way.

“Everyone has to process it. He has to process it himself. We’re still in that grieving stage, the emotional stage, and we’ll be in that for the next few weeks. It won’t be until the next camp where you think about what the future holds and what the next target is. We’ll have conversations as captain and manager and with other teammates and staff, to see where we can be better.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Give it up for Vozinha, Spence and the 2026 World Cup’s cult heroes
Sports.content:
WE CAN BE HEROES

Every World Cup produces cult heroes, icons who make it possible for us to sit back and start misty-eyed recollections by saying: “Do you remember Roger Milla/Saeed Al-Owairan/Keisuke Honda/Paul the Octopus?” Well, the Geopolitics World Cup has not let us down! Here are 10 cult heroes who’ve emerged from this tournament.

Yaya Sithole: a catastrophic start as the South Africa midfielder’s error led to the first goal of the GWC against Mexico, compounded by a second-half red card. Bounced back with a vital display in the win over South Korea, leading his country to the knockout round. Decades from now, people will still be talking about the Yaya Sithole redemption arc. Possibly.

Vozinha: who else? Cape Verde’s players all became cult heroes, but especially the 40-year-old keeper who spent last season in the Portuguese second tier and this summer keeping out Spain as the Blue Sharks went unbeaten in the group stage, then pushed Argentina to extra time in the last 32. Vozinha’s mum: get in line – we’re all in his fan club now.

Djed Spence: a toss-up with Dan “the modern-day header-beast” Burn for England’s cult hero, but let’s give it to the Spurs full-back who transformed from the hapless scourge of Thomas Tuchel’s existence in the group stage to a chin-strapped Cafu in the knockout round. Spence’s slide tackle on Giuliano Simeone (albeit sans chin-strap) will live long in the memory.

View image in fullscreen Djed Spence to the rescue. Photograph: Will Oliver/EPA

Matías Galarza: Paraguay’s most magnificent git was always involved despite rarely trying to play football. Almost every time we saw the midfielder he was moaning, playacting, needling opponents – truly putting the “art” into the dark arts. Also scored against Turkey and later nicked the referee’s watch and strapped it to his own wrist. Timeless ’housery.

Keyne: poor Lamine Yamal, who turned a craggy 19 during the GWC, must be feeling pretty aged considering he’s been usurped by his three-year-old brother. Keyne gurning and giggling in the crowd has delighted fans in Spain and beyond. Considering some of the other people who’ve hogged TV cutaways, the toddler has been a welcome sight.

Iván Barton: Salvadorian referee grabbed the globe’s attention when he sent off Miguel Almirón, bawling at the winger like a mum sending a misbehaving youngster to bed with no dinner. “After review, No 10, Paraguay, covered his mouth! The decision is red card!” No PlayStation either, Miguel!

Eloy Room: move over, Vozinha, and make room for Eloy! Yep, another veteran goalie starred at this GWC as Curaçao bounced back from shipping seven (7) against Germany to hold Ecuador to a 0-0 draw. The 37-year-old Room made 15 saves – a record for a 90-minute World Cup match – to earn the tiny Caribbean island their first ever point.

View image in fullscreen Eloy Room to the rescue. Photograph: Ed Zurga/AP

Danny Murphy: or should it be Bob the cat? The deadpan BBC pundit’s tale of how a family moggy once made a break for freedom inside a Royal Mail van – sparked by Oscar Bobb coming off the bench for Norway – proved so engrossing that viewers demanded, and got, several follow-ups. A purr-fect hydration-break diversion. Honk!

Hossam Hassan: Egypt’s perma-angry, black T-shirted head coach was an intimidating presence – especially paired with his identical twin brother, the team director, Ibrahim Hassan. The pair had a row with Dallas police, led the Pharaohs to the last 16, saw Egypt take a 2-0 lead against Argentina … before the final 15 minutes helped Hossam reach new heights of apoplexy.

Romelu Lukaku: how can Belgium’s record goalscorer be obscure enough for cult-hero status? Well, when you polish off USA USA USA 4-1 and celebrate your 93rd international goal with a Trump dance near the corner flag in the aftermath of Balogungate. Thanks, Big Rom (Bigliest Rom?) – the planet is with you.

View image in fullscreen Romelu Lukaku to the rescue. Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/AP

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Rob Smyth from 8pm BST (3pm EST, 5am AEST) for hot updates from Spain 1-1 Argentina (aet; 4-5 on pens) in the GWC final. The animals below agree, though the punters in New York City disagree. Meanwhile Tom Lutz will be in situ for another liveblog mopping up all other business outside the game, which we’re tempted to call Everything But The Goal.

View image in fullscreen Moo Deng, a two-year-old female pygmy hippopotamus, picks Argentina at Khao Kheow Open Zoo in Thailand Photograph: Anusak Laowilas/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

View image in fullscreen Poty the jaguar sides with the holders too at BioParque, in Rio de Janeiro. Photograph: Tita Barros/Reuters

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“This game will help us for sure – even if you can never fully celebrate a bronze medal. It’s the first [men’s World Cup] medal for 60 years, first [at a men’s] World Cup on foreign soil, and I hope the players can be proud of that at some point. We set ourselves the highest dream to chase, and we were very, very ambitious with our dream to make the final in the World Cup. So it’s very, very painful if you miss out, the pain will stay for a while” – England head coach Thomas Tuchel after overseeing a quite preposterous 6-4 win over France in the Third Place Play-off.

View image in fullscreen England with their bronzes. Photograph: Paul Childs/Reuters

double quotation mark May I be one of the 1,057 pedants to point out that it’s little wonder Brazil lost to Poland in the 1970 TPPO (yesterday’s Football Daily) as they would have been resting players for the next day’s final against Italy (which they won 4-1 to claim their third world crown – Pelé, Carlos Alberto and all that). You must have meant the 1974 TPPO. Easy to be fatigued at this stage of the tournament; just ask Harry Kane” – Jonathan Westwood (and 1,056 others).

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Jonathan Westwood (and the 1,056 others). Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Fifa gives fraud ‘an open door’ with betting, says Council of Europe chief
Sports.content:
Fifa has been accused of providing an “open door to fraud” and allowing political influence to cast doubt on the integrity of the World Cup in a stinging rebuke by the Council of Europe’s secretary general.

In an open letter published to coincide with Sunday’s final, Alain Berset also called for a new integrity framework to be built before the 2030 tournament, which is mainly being staged in Europe, and warned that Fifa was embroiled in a crisis involving money and power.

Berset referenced the scandal surrounding Fifa’s decision to shelve the suspension of the USA striker Folarin Balogun and made apparent allusions to comments made by the Paraguayan senator Celeste Amarilla about Kylian Mbappé and by the former Spanish prime minister Mariano Rajoy about the France team.

“The Fifa World Cup 2026 has raised question after question,” Berset wrote. “A sanction suspended under pressure, within days, with no reasons given. The authority of referees called into question. Racist abuse of players, some of it from elected officials. Betting on every pass, every card, every corner. The celebration will end tonight. The questions will not.”

It is a significant intervention given Fifa and the Council of Europe signed a memorandum of understanding in 2018, which remains valid. The agreement was struck to strengthen their work together on a number of topics, including “human rights, integrity and good governance in sport”. Open criticism of one partner by another is extremely rare.

Berset took aim at Fifa’s deal with ADI Predictstreet, which became the World Cup’s official prediction market partner in April. “Betting has moved from the result of a match to moments a single player can produce without changing the score,” he said. “A bet is won by making others lose. It is an open door to fraud. And this World Cup has opened the door wider.”

In further reference to the lifting of Balogun’s ban by Fifa, which occurred after a phone call to its president, Gianni Infantino, by his US counterpart, Donald Trump, Berset said: “When the rules bend under pressure, every result is open to doubt.”

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino with Donald Trump at the World Cup final reception at Trump Tower on Friday 17 July in New York. Photograph: Ira L Black/Fifa/Getty Images

Infantino has said the decision to revoke Balogun’s ban was taken independently by Fifa’s disciplinary committee “based on the applicable regulations and the specific facts”.

Berset, who is Swiss, proposed a “working dialogue that starts tonight” to begin the “urgent work of strengthening the integrity of sport” before future World Cups. He referenced work by the Council of Europe – which is the continent’s intergovernmental human rights organisation – in creating a binding treaty to keep fans safe three months after the Heysel Stadium disaster in 1985, as well as further legislation set up to tackle doping in athletics and match-fixing.

The letter comes a week and a half after 72 members of the European parliament wrote to the 27 EU-based football associations asking for an investigation into Infantino’s involvement in the Balogun case. It pointed to alleged breaches of political neutrality and suggested Fifa had contravened its own code of ethics.

It does not appear likely that Uefa, European football’s governing body, will formally take the matter further. In June, 50 members of the European parliament wrote to Infantino and the Fifa council requesting an investigation into the awarding of the Fifa peace prize to Trump.

Fifa was contacted for comment.

This past week it was revealed that more that 200 of Fifa’s member associations have formally backed Infantino’s attempt to be re-elected for a fourth term in March.

Sports.title: England 2026 World Cup squad: player-by-player ratings
Sports.content:
Goalkeepers

Jordan Pickford Could he have done better with Enzo Fernández’s equaliser for Argentina? Jude Bellingham certainly thought so. But the man who has made more World Cup finals appearances than any other Englishman made some crucial saves, including a brilliant stop from Nicolas González in the semi-final. 7

Dean Henderson Had to wait until the third-place playoff for some action and ended up conceding four goals despite a strong performance. Will hope to challenge Pickford over next two years. 7

Defenders

Djed Spence Emerged as an unlikely cult hero thanks to some wholehearted performances. He will always be remembered for snubbing Thomas Partey’s handshake and his tackle on Giuliano Simeone against Argentina. 8

Marc Guéhi Somehow wasn’t Thomas Tuchel’s first-choice initially, although that was rectified after the Croatia game. England’s most consistent and reliable defender – the way he handled Erling Haaland was a masterclass. 8

John Stones Arrived painfully short of match fitness and it showed in the opening game against Croatia. Much improved when called upon in the quarter- and semi-finals. A huge asset when he plays. 7

Ezri Konsa A few shaky moments during the group stage but recovered well and filled in capably at right-back when needed. At 28, young enough to be there again in four years. 7

View image in fullscreen Dan Burn’s headed block from this Raúl Jiménez bicycle kick cleared the halfway line. Photograph: Ulises Ruiz/AFP/Getty Images

Dan Burn Showed his limitations against Argentina. But he will always have those two epic appearances off the bench against Mexico and Norway. No one will forget the clearing headers so powerful they ended up in the opposition’s half. 7

Nico O’Reilly Had his strongest game against Norway in the quarter-final when he was at his marauding best. Will be disappointed not to have scored and to have been on the pitch as a substitute when Argentina instigated their semi-final comeback. 6

Reece James Such a good player when fit, which is sadly far too rare. Missed most of the tournament owing to a hamstring injury and England suffered when he went off against Argentina. 6

Trevoh Chalobah The Chelsea player was a surprise choice to replace Tino Livramento, who pulled out injured at the last minute. Managed only six minutes against France in the end. 6

Jarell Quansah Brought in to solve the right-back conundrum against Panama, he was doing well until the rush of blood against Mexico and subsequent red card. Recalled for the France game and had to be replaced. 5

Midfielders

Jude Bellingham Showed his supreme quality when it mattered and could not be more committed to his country’s cause, even if his rocky relationship with Tuchel had to be carefully managed. 9

Elliot Anderson Didn’t allow himself to be distracted by his £116m move to Manchester City and grew as the tournament progressed. Ran his heart out against Norway and Argentina. 8

View image in fullscreen Morgan Rogers (left) crossed for Anthony Gordon to put England ahead against Argentina. Photograph: Julian Finney/FIFA/Getty Images

Morgan Rogers Made the most of his limited minutes in unfamiliar roles. Showed what a good player he is by playing as one of the two central midfielders against Norway before setting up Anthony Gordon from the right wing against Argentina. 8

Declan Rice Clearly affected by the hamstring and back problems that marred the second half of his season with Arsenal, even if his effort – as ever – could not be faulted. Needs a long rest to recharge his batteries but may not get one. 6

Eberechi Eze Could not have the impact he would have wished for in four substitute appearances before starting against France. Did a decent job in central midfield against Panama but was largely on the periphery when given a chance on the left in the quarter-final. 6

Jordan Henderson Spent 12 minutes on the pitch, in a historic appearance against Panama when he became the first England men’s player to appear at seven major international tournaments. But managed to get booked against Mexico as a substitute and break an arm celebrating the win. 5

Forwards

Bukayo Saka Three goals and three assists despite playing through the pain of an achilles injury was a courageous effort from Arsenal’s talisman. It was a huge surprise not to see him come off the bench against Argentina and he showed what England were missing against France. 8

Anthony Gordon A quiet start having been preferred to Rashford before responding magnificently to being dropped. Three assists and a goal against Argentina showed why Barcelona were so keen to sign him. 8

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane’s two goals against the Democratic Republic of the Congo saved England from an early exit. Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA

Harry Kane Sadly his tournament will be remembered for a largely anonymous display against Argentina rather than rescuing England against the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Will he ever have a better chance to win the World Cup? 8

Marcus Rashford Made a good start to his third World Cup by coming off the bench to score against Croatia, and started against Panama. But wasn’t seen again until England were chasing the game against Argentina in injury time. 6

Ivan Toney Sat on the bench until Lautaro Martínez’s goal in added time of the semi-final. Could not make an impact in the three minutes he was given but did well against France. 6

Ollie Watkins Largely a frustrated spectator despite his heroics in the Euro 2024 semi-final and arriving here in a rich vein of form. A half on the left flank against France and a brief appearance against Panama were scant reward. 6

Noni Madueke Some promising moments but lacked end product in his four starts and had slipped down the pecking order by the semi-final. Needs to be much more clinical at this level. 5

Did not play: James Trafford and Kobbie Mainoo

Sports.title: Fifa to announce record $15bn World Cup revenue, smashing expectations
Sports.content:
Fifa will announce record $15bn (£11.2bn) revenues from this summer’s World Cup, significantly exceeding the targets set before the tournament.

Fifa’s member associations were informed of the boost in income by Gianni Infantino on Saturday. Originally the governing body had projected $11bn in earnings. Sources have indicated that hospitality and ticketing, especially through the steeply priced secondary market, account for a significant amount of the increase. Fifa takes 15% from the buyer and another 15% from the seller on the secondary market.

It is likely that football associations will reap the benefits of Fifa’s expanded World Cup pot, although details are yet to be finalised. The financial situation will come as a boost to Infantino, who will feel it further shores up his position after a controversy-ridden month in the US, Canada and Mexico.

There was widespread fury after Fifa was perceived to have bowed to pressure from Donald Trump in suspending the red card given to Folarin Balogun, the US striker, against Bosnia and Herzegovina in the last 32. Fifa has said the decision was taken independently by its disciplinary committee but that has continued to fester among European FAs in particular. Infantino has nevertheless received more than 200 pledges of support from Fifa’s member associations for his re-election in March. The prospect of extra funds from bumper World Cup revenue is likely to dissuade some FAs from making any discontent public.

Such a bonanza may also increase the chances of the US hosting another edition in the near future. The next World Cup available for bids is the 2038 tournament. At a reception on Friday, Trump confirmed his country’s eagerness for a repeat performance. “You should choose the United States of America again,” he said. “This time we will leave Canada and Mexico out.” The US has also held talks with Fifa about hosting the Club World Cup in 2029.

On Saturday evening, VIP and hospitality packages for Sunday’s final between Spain and Argentina, which was played in New Jersey, were still listed on Fifa’s ticketing portal. Tickets for the “trophy lounge” were retailing at $34,500 per person.

Sports.title: America’s World Cup report card: some As for atmosphere, but F for affordability
Sports.content:
Come rain or smokescreen, Sunday will bring the 2026 World Cup to its bombastic end. The load-bearer of the co-hosting North American trio, the United States held 78 of the tournament’s matches across its 11 host cities. Only two contests remain: the third-place game in Miami, and the big one in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Before the dust truly settles and focus shifts to the six-nation, three-continent centennial in 2030, how did the United States fare in its second swing at hosting a men’s World Cup?

Stadiums

Depending on what you’re looking for, best in class. Few venues have “charm” in the traditional sense, but these sprawling NFL venues packed in plenty of fans, with many designed to retain sound to harness atmosphere. That said, none seem to have figured out how to adequately keep a concourse congregation flowing, with those corridors hardly expanded to account for so many people in one building. B+

Transport

This was an anticipated drawback of holding this tournament in the US, as the nation rebuilt itself throughout the 20th century with clear priorities for the automobile. Some cities stepped up their public transportation options with ad‑hoc buses; others used those initiatives to further eat into riders’ spending budgets. Hours spent slowly progressing to venues, and even more slowly when leaving, were equally costly. D+

Affordability

Do we even need to explain this one? The expectations for ticket pricing made public in United 26’s bid book were in line with what we’ve come to expect for World Cups, with inflation largely justifying modest increases from tournament to tournament. Instead, the 2026 World Cup became an outlier for event pricing of nearly any kind – the first that most of the world could never afford to attend.

Fifa admitted this was a rare chance to spawn an ATM from the tournament’s rib, and that the ludicrously priced inventory wouldn’t be sustainable for future installments on other continents. An unapologetic slap in the face of USsoccer fans. Once Fifa set this precedent, every other stakeholder in the tournament – transport, food and beverage vendors, merchandisers, parking lot operators, taxis, everyone – followed suit. F

View image in fullscreen Even if you had a ticket to a World Cup match in Philadelphia, the price of parking was no small feat. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

Hospitality

On the one hand, the displays of community were incredibly touching. No matter how overpriced the lager was, it was common to see traveling fans from all over the world clinking cups before and after the match. Fifa’s legion of volunteers were smiling faces in neon tracksuits, awfully helpful and welcoming at every turn.

On the other hand, not all fans were quite so well accommodated. Referees and team staffers were among those turned away by Trump administration decisions. That precedent also left the general fan from a Trump-banned nation without a chance of getting around policies. The rationale for those rejections was incredibly flimsy, yet Fifa stood beside the man in the White House.

It will be impossible not to wonder how different the support of Côte d’Ivoire, Haiti, Iran and Senegal could have been had the tourist accessibility of the 1994 World Cup been replicated. A for the spirit fostered by those who could make it, but F for the unprecedented barriers set before qualifiers and customers alike.

Atmosphere

The category with the biggest discrepancies between the best-in-class and the rest. Some – Seattle, Philadelphia and Kansas City – cemented an identity of being organic and sustainable soccer cities. The “World Cup village” atmosphere so many fans covet was alive and well, with accessible public watch parties, signage and flags lining streets, and a constant buzz of excitement that the world’s eyes found their neck of the woods. Others, like Boston – the second capital of Scotland – and the Bay Area either embraced their temporary occupants or had plenty of space and opportunities for locals to keep the party going between matchdays.

Others, especially those whose stadiums weren’t in or adjacent to the city center, really struggled to harness the tournament’s potential. It turns out being an hour or two away from the action feels just as invigorating to some as watching a game from their sofa. Texas seemed especially agnostic despite being one of two states with multiple host cities, with dispatches from Dallas and Houston reading equally blase. The roadshow has already packed up, and many in some of these cities will hardly recognize what came through. B-

Sports.title: World Cup fans brand FIFA's first-ever halftime show a 'disaster' as Madonna and Bieber's bizarre spectacle divides billions
Sports.content:
Have you got a story? Email tips@dailymail.com

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

World Cup fans branded FIFA's controversial first-ever World Cup halftime show starring Madonna and Justin Bieber a 'disaster' on Sunday - as the spectacle divided viewers around the world.

The futuristic segment began with Madonna, 67, singing her 2000 hit Music, accompanied by giddy Brazilian World Cup legends Ronaldo Nazario and Ronaldinho.

The toned music legend was dressed head-to-toe in Saint Laurent, wowing in a pink satin teddy jacket and corset, mini shorts and lace-up boots, paired with stockings as she embraced the soccer icons, before they drove her out into the stadium.

The unlikely trio then posed up on the grass and smiled at the crowds.

Bieber, 32, made a starkly different impact on the crowd as he stepped out with nothing but a guitar to sing a World Cup themed version of his song, Everything Hallelujah.

The singer was bizarrely subbed onto the pitch by Jason Sudeikis, playing his manager alter-ego Ted Lasso.

The star looked relaxed as he casually walked onto the pitch before belting out his hit track, adding the final line, 'it's the World Cup, Hallelujah' - with fans left baffled by his song choice.

One fan gave the damning verdict, 'What a disaster this halftime show was. Pre-recorded stuff, no collaborations or surprising moments. Where was Madonna at the end? She could have sung a few lines with Shakira... everything was so weird. So much hype for nothing.'

Madonna and Justin Bieber's performances during the controversial first-ever FIFA World Cup halftime show divided fans on Sunday

Yet making clear the division, a second viewer wrote, 'I dislike a lot of things that FIFA does... but THAT halftime show was pretty spectacular.'

Another wrote, 'Who was behind the concept for that haltfime show? Chat GPT?'

Bieber's downbeat song choice was undoubtedly one of the major talking points of the performance, with one fan writing, 'Justin Bieber was unfortunately the worst part of the World Cup halftime show.'

Another penned, 'Justin Bieber Hallelujah but this was not the right song choice for the half time show.'

A third typed, 'Buzz killer. Totally sucked . Why choose that song that nobody knows . Beyond me ….' while another wrote, 'terrible song choice.'

Others praised Bieber's performance, writing, 'Justin Bieber looked and sounded great at the World Cup halftime show today!

'Glad he's cleaned up his act!

'Best performance. He knows how to switch people’s moods in a second. That’s extremely difficult to do, most performers couldn’t.'

Shakira returned to the World Cup stage as she flaunted her toned abs in a pink and yellow sequined bodysuit to perform her hit Dai Dai, with Burna Boy, while K-pop sensations BTS regaled the crowd with Dynamite.

Spain and Argentina were still 0-0 at halftime, with superstars Lionel Messi and Lamine Yamal forced to share the stage as soccer is given a slice of the Super Bowl treatment

Billions of fans tuned into Sunday's game as Messi and Co bid to secure a second successive World Cup triumph.

As well as a halftime show, the World Cup final also included a closing ceremony that featured performances and appearances from Post Malone, Cruise, Nicole Scherzinger, influencer IShowSpeed, Oscar winner Jennifer Hudson, Robbie Williams and Italian singer Laura Pausini.

Stars including Tom Cruise, Timothee Chalamet, Kylie Jenner, Matt Damon and Adrien Brody joined the crowds for the final.

Spanish actor Javier Bardem, skiing legend Lindsey Vonn and actress Julia Garner were also in attendance for the FIFA Gold Carpet event ahead of the final.

Cruise's specific role is unclear, with FIFA describing it only as a 'special appearance.' But soccer chiefs say the ceremony will pay tribute to all 48 nations from the tournament.

World Cup final day got off to a chaotic start at MetLife Stadium with fans forced to wait for hours outside of the venue amid reports of technological glitches scanning tickets and security staff unsure of how to manage the crowds.

Organizers this week urged fans lucky enough to have a ticket to arrive up to four hours before the start of the game at the 80,000-seater stadium in New Jersey, a short drive outside of Manhattan, for Sunday's showdown between Spain and Argentina.

As the build-up to the game expected to be watched by billions around the world ramped up, fans were waiting for over four hours to have their tickets scanned in order to enter the stadium for the showpiece game.

The attendance of President Donald Trump meant that airport-style security measures were also being enforced for everyone making their way inside of the venue.

But the delays were compounded amid reports of glitches in FIFA's ticket-scanning system, meaning those who were fortunate enough to be at the front of the long lines still faced frustrating delays.

Daily Mail also witnessed tensions simmering between fans, media members and security staff, with officials on the ground telling anyone who complained: 'Take it up with FIFA'.

The game is set to be the most expensive to attend in the history of sport - on Sunday morning, the cheapest ticket available on most resale websites was starting at around $7,000.

FIFA encouraged fans to arrive early in order to participate in the World Cup closing ceremony, scheduled to begin around 90 minutes before the game itself kicks off.

But it is standard procedure for fans to arrive early for additional security checks whenever Trump attends a sporting event - and he has made it to plenty in his second term as President, ranging from the Ryder Cup to the Super Bowl.

Soccer greats such as Brazil World Cup winner Ronaldo, former England captain John Terry and former Argentina player Diego Simeone all appeared carefree as they entered the stadium in good time before the game.

There were plenty of fans who were determined not to let the chaos ruin their day, too. Thousands of Argentina fans have made the journey to the stadium for what will likely be star man Lionel Messi's last ever appearance in a World Cup at the age of 39.

Argentina are narrow underdogs against Spain, the European champions, despite being the holders after winning the 2022 tournament in Qatar.

Sports.title: Ian Wright hits out at 'ridiculous and poor' World Cup final pitch at the MetLife Stadium - and that was BEFORE extravagant half-time show featuring Justin Bieber and Shakira
Sports.content:
Ian Wright has hit out at the state of the World Cup final pitch, dubbing it 'ridiculous, bobbly and poor'.

The MetLife Stadium in New Jersey has come in for criticism throughout this summer's tournament, and once again appeared dry and patchy as Spain took on Argentina on Sunday night.

A number of instances saw stars, including the great Lionel Messi, struggle to control the ball as it bobbled along the uneven surface.

And, speaking during ITV's half-time coverage of the clash, Wright didn't hold any punches while assessing the venue for the biggest game in the footballing calendar.

He said: 'For a World Cup final this pitch is ridiculous, it's poor, it (the game) shouldn't be on it.

'I think Spain are playing and showing how good they are because even on a bobbly, dry pitch like this, they're doing really good stuff.

Ian Wright has hit out at the state of the World Cup final pitch, dubbing it 'ridiculous, bobbly and poor'

The turf in New Jersey has come in for criticism throughout the tournament

'I think Argentina will stay in it but, for me, Spain are passing it all over the place. It's only a matter of time before they take one of these chances.'

The 80,000-capacity MetLife sits on the outskirts of New York, which was hit by severe thunderstorms causing flooding in the hours ahead of kick-off in the sweltering east coast sunshine.

Yet the pitch had been deemed subpar by players and managers long before it was hit by rainfall.

It predominantly consists of natural grass, but the turf has been installed over an artificial surface underneath which can make it 'dry out' quickly when temperatures soar.

Brazil star Vinicius Jr was one of the stars who took issue with the surface earlier in the tournament, telling reporters after his country's 1-1 draw with Morocco: 'Because of the weather and the heat, the grass dries out quickly and the game ends up being very slow.

'We can't build up a rhythm. That makes things difficult because we want to move the ball from one side to the other and this disrupts our game.'

French coach Didier Deschamps later criticised the venue, saying: 'The pitch in New York was really tough - it took a lot out of the players' muscles.'

Wright's comments came moments before the broadcaster's coverage cut to the highly-anticipated half-time show, which was facilitated by a controversial interval of 30 minutes.

A star-studded half-time show featured performances from Shakira (pictured) and Justin Bieber

It featured a star-studded lineup including performances by Shakira, Burna Boy, Justin Bieber and Madonna - and even cameo appearances from footballing royalty Ronaldinho and Ronaldo.

Madonna kickstarted the performance with her hit 'Music', walking out onto the field with 2002 World Cup winners and Brazilian legends Ronaldo and Ronaldinho.

Bieber was then introduced by Ted Lasso for a short, slow acoustic performance while a montage of the tournament was playing on the big screens around the 80,000-seater stadium.

Shakira later returned and injected some energy into the show before the performance came to an end and the preparation for the second half quickly restarted.

Yet ITV's panel of pundits were left less than impressed by the show - as was Wayne Rooney on the BBC.

Keane said: 'A bit of anti-climax but I think the people in the stadium probably enjoyed it more than us. It was nice to see Shakira.'

Wright added: '(Justin) Bieber should have done something a bit more upbeat to liven us up a bit.'

While Rooney reflected bluntly: 'My favourite bit of the half time show was when it finished… I like all of them artists but I thought it was crap.'

A host of stars flooded to New Jersey for the climax of this summer's tournament.

Before kick-off, Top Gun and Mission Impossible superstar Tom Cruise took to the pitch to give a motivational pre-match speech. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump was pictured sat in his luxury suite next to FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

Celebrity couple Timothee Chalament and Kylie Jenner were also snapped in the stands, as were Mick Jagger, Pharrell Williams, Victoria Beckham and Will Ferrell.
